doc.title: Konitz Lee — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

title: Lars Gullin
summary: Konitz remembers the Swedish baritone player as a marvelous musician, with stories of his drug problems.

story.theme_name: Drink, drugs and the bandstand's casualties
story.community_name: Drugs and drink on the bandstand and the road

blocks.x: I want to talk about a couple of people. I’m looking through this discography and not long after those sessions you did some stuff in Germany with Lars Gullin and Hans Koller. You knew Lars Gullin fairly well right?
And played his music more than once on records. What are your thoughts about him as a player and composer?

He was a marvelous musician. Classical pianist, classical composer, and a very nice composer of jazz tunes, and a player I think that was very influenced by the Tristano people and I think particularly by Gerry Mulligan. He had that kind of sound and feeling I think in his baritone playing. I have a memory of him coming to my hotel room in Stockholm and looking around at my electric razor and whatever else I had out on the table. He said, “You have nice things.” [Laughs] He was a sweet guy.
Unfortunately he has some terrible drug problems.

That was the un-sweet part. I remember I had a pair of sunglasses that I had painted black inside so I could really stand up and not see when playing, because I usually close my eyes and don’t see anyway, and I remember standing [where] I could see him on the bandstand in this club and I said, “try these” and oh man, did he like those glasses. He might’ve made a pair.
